description.summary: Al-Mi'raj is a yellow, hare- or rabbit-like creature with a single black horn described in medieval Arabic 'wonders' literature, most famously in Zakariya al-Qazwini's 13th-century Marvels of Things Created. It is said to live on Dragon Island in the Indian Ocean and to drive all other beasts to flight at the sight of it.
description.full: Al-Mi'raj (Arabic: ٱلْمِعْرَاج, al-miʿrāj) is a mythical creature of medieval Arabic literature. Its earliest sustained description is in the cosmographical work ʿAjāʾib al-Makhlūqāt wa Gharāʾib al-Mawjūdāt ('Marvels of Things Created and Miraculous Aspects of Things Existing', also known as The Wonders of Creation) by the 13th-century Persian polymath Zakariya al-Qazwini (c. 1203–1283). Qazwini describes the al-mi'raj as a yellow beast resembling a hare or rabbit in size and shape, distinguished by a single prominent black horn rising from its head like that of a unicorn. The animal is said to inhabit a place called Jazīrat al-Tinnīn ('Dragon Island' or 'Sea-Serpent Island') in the Indian Ocean. According to a version of the legend of Iskandar (Alexander the Great), the islanders gave the creature to him as a gift after he defeated a dragon menacing their flocks. Despite its small, otherwise rabbit-like form, the al-mi'raj is described as fearsome: all wild beasts flee at the sight of it, and Arabic and Persian sources treat it as dangerous to humans as well. The oldest surviving illustrated manuscripts of Qazwini's text — including Bavarian State Library Cod. arab. 464, dated to c. 1279/1280 or 1377 — preserve early depictions of the creature. Qazwini's al-Mi'raj sits within a wider Arabic-Persian tradition of horned hares and 'unicorns' that overlaps with the European jackalope motif and with the karkadann.

etymology.origin: Arabic; manuscript transmission yields several variants (al-miʿrāj, ʿarāj, baqrāj, al-Maharāj).
etymology.meaning: The standard form al-miʿrāj is unrelated to the better-known Islamic term miʿrāj for the Prophet Muhammad's ascent to heaven; the creature's name is treated as a proper noun.
etymology.first_use: 13th century, in Qazwini's Marvels of Things Created.

Despite its size, said to be highly aggressive and capable of defeating much larger adversaries.

origins.cultural_roots: Arabic and Persian cosmographical and 'wonders of creation' literature of the 13th century, drawing on earlier Greek, Mesopotamian, and Indian sources.
origins.earliest_accounts: Qazwini's Marvels of Things Created (c. 1260), as preserved in 13th- and 14th-century manuscripts.
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to the Alexander Romance via the Iskandar / Dragon Island episode and to the broader medieval network of horned-hare and unicorn motifs.

timeline.event: Zakariya al-Qazwini composes ʿAjāʾib al-Makhlūqāt wa Gharāʾib al-Mawjūdāt (Marvels of Things Created)
timeline.significance: Earliest sustained description of the al-Mi'raj

timeline.significance: Preserves early visual depictions of the al-Mi'raj

history.modern_era: The al-Mi'raj survives chiefly through manuscript scholarship and modern fantasy and gaming reuse. It is a stock 'monster manual' creature in Western fantasy bestiaries and continues to draw scholarly attention as a node in the wider horned-hare motif.

documentary.description: Qazwini's textual and illustrated entry describing the al-Mi'raj.
documentary.analysis: Earliest sustained primary source; preserved in multiple 13th- and 14th-century manuscripts including Cod. arab. 464.

scientific.name: Mythologised horned hare
scientific.description: The al-Mi'raj is best understood as a literary horned-hare motif, related to other Eurasian horned-hare and unicorn traditions and partly underwritten by the real phenomenon of leporids with the cottontail papillomavirus, which produces horn-like keratin growths.
evidence_cited: Modern documentation of papillomavirus-induced 'horns' on hares and rabbits

skeptical.name: Wonders-literature creature
skeptical.description: Modern scholars treat the al-Mi'raj as a literary creature of the marvels tradition rather than a zoological claim. Its placement on the unmapped 'Dragon Island' marks it as part of the conventional 'edges of the world' geography of medieval cosmography.
evidence_cited: Use of Dragon Island as a generic Arabic 'island of marvels'

stories: Iskandar receives the al-Mi'raj as a gift after killing the dragon of Dragon Island
